subject: ventures/junk-car-buyer-offer-calculator
professional: a small junk-car buyer or salvage-yard owner who quotes cars over the phone; they check first that hulk value is weight over a 2,000 lb net ton times the yard's quote, that the converter is priced separately, that tow cost reflects the miles they actually drive, and that a car with no converter or no sellable parts is priced at zero for those lines, not at an example figure

evidence.correctness: Ran calc.mjs through node on three cases and recomputed each by hand. Default car: (3200-250)/2000*220 = 324.50 hulk, 450*0.60*0.87 = 234.90 parts, revenue 709.40, costs 95+40+25+28+37.5+30 = 255.50, net 453.90, max offer 353.90; tool matches. 2,700 lb compact (no parts, $180/ton, $120 converter, 15 mi tow, ask $150, target $75): hulk 243, costs 80+40+25+30 = 175, net 188, max offer 113, profit at ask 38, break-even scrap (150+75-(188-243))/1.35 = $207.41/ton, max tow 15+(38-75)/3 = 2.67 mi; tool matches all. 4,700 lb pickup (600 lb pulled, $250/ton, $300 converter, $800 parts at 50%, 40 mi, 30 days): hulk 512.50, parts 348, costs 385, net 775.50; tool matches. The default $220/ton is above the $145-210/ton range that US junk-car buyer sites published for 2025 (web search, junkcarmedics.com and junkcarreaper.com, marketing-adjacent sources), but the page says defaults are placeholders. Not 4: a cleared or mistyped field silently becomes the example value (blank converter -> $150 added, '3,2OO' lbs -> 3,200), and the sell-through limit says 'never at these figures' when there are no parts to sell even though the ask already works.
evidence.completeness: README and page claim: max offer, profit at ask, break-even offer, scrap-price limit, farthest tow, parts sell-through limit, five ladders, CSV download, warnings, usage opt-out. All ran end to end via analyze() and toCsv(); ladders monotone; CSV header and rows produced; bad input (weight 0, parts heavier than car, fee >100%, negative) returns warnings and no result. No stubs or TODOs in 116-line calc.mjs.
evidence.verification: node --test '*.test.mjs': 23 tests pass (Node 22.23.4). Tests recompute the default car by hand and check each solved limit reproduces the target profit, which is good. But 4 of 5 seeded mutants survived via quality_mutate.py: the buy verdict (profitAtAsk >= target -> > 0) which drives the page headline 'Take it at the ask', the sell-through zero branch, the storage warning threshold, and floor -> ceil on the counter. Only the 2000 -> 2240 ton constant was caught. No test covers blank input or the no-parts case.
evidence.craft: Read calc.mjs, index.html script, calc.test.mjs, page.test.mjs. Pure functions, small and readable, limits solved in closed form. Defects: silent fallback to DEFAULTS for non-finite input in both analyze (calc.mjs:94) and the page's opts() (index.html:143); breakEvenSellThrough conflates 'no parts' with 'impossible' (calc.mjs:77); headline rounds maxOffer with money() (353.9 -> $354) while the counter warning floors it ($353).
evidence.claims: Checked: 'Nothing is uploaded' (page.test asserts no fetch/XHR/beacon; index imports only ./calc.mjs and ./usage.mjs) backed; 'each limit is solved and tests check it reproduces the target' backed by calc.test.mjs; disclaimer (no warranty, not advice, no SLA) present on page and README; defaults labelled 'placeholders, not your crusher's quote'; 'Not decided' section lists title, licensing, converter law, price swings, taxes; usage events named equal those recorded. Source llms.txt points to the old github.io host but the served https://marisstella.app/junk-car-buyer-offer-calculator/llms.txt is rewritten correctly (source-only, not a defect). No overclaim found.
evidence.fitness: Walked the job: a buyer gets a phone call, types weight, yard quote, converter, ask, and gets a counter. Works for a single car. Gaps in the first hour: clearing a field (e.g. converter missing/stolen) silently re-adds the example $150; only one-way tow miles are costed, so a buyer driving their own truck out empty and back loaded undercounts mileage by about half; no way to keep a quote list or compare cars; 'never at these figures' for a car with no parts is confusing.
evidence.domain: Method matches the standard work-backward offer a yard owner uses (scrap weight x price per net ton + converter + parts net of fees - tow, title, disposal, storage, labour, haul - margin). Departures: tow cost assumes one-way billed miles (fine for a hired tow quoting loaded miles, wrong for own-truck deadhead); hulk weight is curb weight minus pulled parts with no deduction for tires and fluids removed at depollution; no complete-vs-incomplete car price differential. These are stated-limit level, not method errors.

defects.what: A cleared or mistyped field silently takes the example value: leaving the converter blank for a car whose converter is gone adds $150 to the offer; a blank weight prices a 3,200 lb car. No warning is shown.
analyze() repeats the same silent fallback for non-finite raw values instead of warning
The buy verdict that sets the headline ('Take it at the ask' vs 'Counter') is untested between 0 and the target profit: mutating >= target to > 0 passes all 23 tests; 4 of 5 seeded mutants survived
breakEvenSellThrough returns NaN when partsRetail is 0, shown as 'never at these figures' even when the ask already clears the target
Tow is costed on one-way miles only; a buyer using their own truck drives the empty leg too, so mileage cost is about half of real
Headline rounds the max offer to nearest dollar ($354 for 353.9) while the counter warning floors it ($353), so the page shows two different 'most you can offer' numbers

verdict: The arithmetic is right: three cars recomputed by hand (default 3,200 lb car, a 2,700 lb compact with no parts, a 4,700 lb pickup) match the tool to the cent, including the closed-form break-even scrap price and farthest tow, and the method is the work-backward offer a yard owner uses. Claims are backed, the disclaimer and placeholder wording are present, and the served llms.txt is correct. It does not meet the bar because verification is 2: four of five seeded mutants survive 23 green tests, including the buy verdict that drives the headline. The worst defect is input handling: a blank or mistyped field silently becomes the example value, so a buyer who clears the converter field for a car with no converter is told to pay $150 more. Correctness, completeness, craft, claims and domain 3; verification and fitness 2.
